title: Multi-Modal Search: Text and Image Together

questions.q: How does CLIP make cross-modal retrieval possible?
options: It trains a text encoder and an image encoder jointly with contrastive loss — pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart — so both land in the same 512- or 768-dimensional vector space
It converts images to text captions and then does text search
It uses full-text search over image EXIF metadata
It stores images and text in separate indexes and joins them at query time
questions.explain: CLIP's contrastive training produces text and image encoders in the same coordinate system, so a text query vector can directly retrieve images by proximity — the foundational insight behind multi-modal search.

questions.q: Why must you embed query text with the same model's text encoder that produced the stored vectors?
options: It is just a convention; any encoder works
Mixing encoders from different CLIP checkpoints produces meaningless distance comparisons — like comparing meters with feet without conversion
SQL Server enforces encoder matching at insert time
Different encoders produce different file formats
questions.explain: Vectors from different model checkpoints live in unrelated coordinate systems; mixing them is equivalent to comparing meters with feet without conversion, so query text must use the same checkpoint's text encoder.

questions.q: What distance metric is natural for CLIP vectors in SQL Server, and why?
options: Hamming, because CLIP outputs binary codes
Euclidean, because CLIP vectors are sparse
Manhattan, because it is faster to compute
Cosine via VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', ...) because CLIP encoders produce unit-normalized vectors by default
questions.explain: CLIP vectors are unit-normalized by default, so cosine similarity is the natural metric — and pre-normalizing at embed time lets the database compute it as a cheaper dot product.

questions.q: When is early fusion valid, and when must you use late fusion instead?
options: Late fusion is deprecated in favor of early fusion
Fusion is never needed because one index handles everything

Early fusion (averaging query vectors) works only when text and image embeddings share the same model and dimensionality; late fusion (separate searches, score combination) is the safe default when embedding models differ — e.g. 1536-d OpenAI text with 512-d CLIP image vectors
Early fusion is always valid regardless of model
questions.explain: Early fusion's weighted average only makes sense inside one shared space; with unrelated spaces (different models/dimensions), each modality needs its own search and the scores combine afterward — late fusion.

questions.q: Why is score normalization required before combining modality scores in late fusion, and what is RRF's advantage?
options: Normalization is optional; raw scores are always comparable across models

Different models produce scores with different statistical distributions — e.g. CLIP image-to-image similarities cluster in a narrower range — so raw combination biases fusion; RRF is rank-based and therefore inherently distribution-agnostic
Normalization doubles query latency so it is usually skipped
RRF requires normalized scores as input
questions.explain: A cosine of 0.7 means different things in different embedding spaces, so combining raw scores biases fusion toward whichever modality produces larger values; RRF avoids this entirely by fusing ranks instead of scores.
